citation: Guidi, G., Dominici, F., Gilmour, J., Butler, K., Bell, E., Delaney, S., & Bargagli-Stoffi, F. J. (2024). Environmental Burden of United States Data Centers in the Artificial Intelligence Era. arXiv preprint arXiv:2411.09786.
region: National US (contiguous US; state and balancing-authority level)
research_question: How much electricity do US data centers consume, from which fuel sources, and what greenhouse gas emissions and carbon intensity are attributable to them?
methodology: 2,132 US data centers operating September 2023 to August 2024. Facility data came from Baxtel (a proprietary dataset of 2,144 data centers), web scraping (datacenters.com, 1,182 facilities), and OpenStreetMap building footprints. Facilities were matched to EPA eGRID 2022 power plant data (3,318 plants above 25 MW) using WattTime balancing-authority boundaries. Electricity use was estimated assuming a uniform 0.75 uptime, and a consequential analysis appears in the Supplementary Material.
key_findings: Estimated consumption of 192.64 TWh, about 4.59% of 2022 US electricity use (abstract: more than 4%). Emissions of 105.59 million metric tons CO2e, 2.18% of US energy-related emissions; the consequential analysis gives 101.21 million metric tons. Weighted average carbon intensity of 548 gCO2e/kWh, about 48% above the US average of 369 gCO2e/kWh. Fossil fuels supplied more than 56% of data center electricity, nuclear about 21%, and renewables about 22%. Virginia had the most facilities (301), and Virginia, Texas, and Oregon had the highest attributable emissions. Water: Not reported.
stated_limitations: Uptime (capacity utilization) is assumed to be 0.75 for every data center. EPA reporting thresholds mean smaller or lower-emission power plants may be missing from eGRID. Facility-specific operating data is closely guarded by the industry and was not available.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "Our findings reveal that data centers accounted for more than 4% of total US electricity consumption" (Abstract; PDF page number not visible via web fetch)

citation: Shehabi, A., Smith, S. J., Hubbard, A., Newkirk, A., Lei, N., Siddik, M. A. B., Holecek, B., Koomey, J., Masanet, E., & Sartor, D. (2024). 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, LBNL-2001637.
research_question: How much electricity, water, and greenhouse gas emissions are associated with US data center operations from 2014 to 2028?
methodology: A bottom-up model scales equipment-level data to national totals, using shipment data to estimate the installed base each year (p. 15). The time horizon is 2014 to 2028 (p. 16). Values after 2023 are scenario ranges that vary GPU shipments, AI server operating hours and power draw, and cooling efficiency, and from 2024 onward they rest on equipment shipment forecasts (pp. 6-7, 17).
key_findings: Electricity: about 60 TWh in 2014-2016 (p. 6), rising to 176 TWh in 2023, or 4.4% of US electricity (p. 7). 2028 projection: 325-580 TWh, or 6.7%-12.0% of US consumption, equal to 74-132 GW at 50% utilization (p. 7). Direct water: 21.2 billion liters in 2014 and 66 billion liters in 2023, with hyperscale and colocation accounting for 84% in 2023; hyperscale facilities are projected to use 60-124 billion liters in 2028 (p. 57). Indirect water footprint of nearly 800 billion liters and GHG emissions of 74 billion kg CO2e for 2023 (p. 58). Total direct water for all US data centers in 2028: Not reported (only the hyperscale segment is projected). Note: p. 58 restates 2023 electricity use as approximately 178 TWh, versus 176 TWh on p. 7.
stated_limitations: Direct energy data is lacking in a sector with rapidly changing technology (p. 8). The model relies on limited public data and proprietary market data (p. 8). Estimates from 2024 onward depend on shipment forecasts (p. 17). Because facility-level data is unavailable, the report applies a single grid mix when calculating indirect water and emissions (p. 58).
verbatim_quote_with_page: "reaching 176 TWh by 2023, representing 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption." (p. 7)

citation: Electric Power Research Institute [Blanford, G., Wilson, T., Bistline, J., & Johnson, N.] (2026). Powering Intelligence: Updated U.S. Data Center Scenarios. Electric Power Research Institute (ESCA brief summarizing the white paper 'Powering Intelligence: Updated Scenarios of U.S. Data Center Electricity Use and Power Strategies').
research_question: How much electricity might US data centers consume by 2030, which states will be most affected, and which generation resources would meet that load?
methodology: Scenarios built from state-level data on operational capacity, construction in progress, and announced plans. Projects are grouped as under construction, in advanced planning, or in early planning, each with different execution assumptions. Baseline 2024, horizon 2030. Covers small- and large-scale data centers plus cryptocurrency mining. Results are compared with EPRI's 2024 projections and with LBNL's December 2024 report. Sample size: Not reported.
key_findings: Data centers would use 9%-17% of US electricity by 2030, up from 4%-5% today, about 60% above EPRI's 2024 projection. Annual use rises from roughly 177-192 TWh in 2024 to about 380-790 TWh in 2030. Nominal IT capacity grows from 35-44 GW (2024) to 56-132 GW (2030). Virginia's share of state electricity goes from above 20% today to 39%-57% by 2030. In the Medium scenario, eight states exceed 20% by 2030 (Virginia, Oregon, Iowa, Nebraska, Nevada, Wyoming, Arizona, Indiana). Data centers used 184 TWh in 2024, compared with 12 TWh for EV charging. Under current policies, least-cost procurement favors natural gas.
stated_limitations: Announced capacity is a pipeline indicator, not a near-term peak forecast. Peak effects depend on non-IT loads, ramp-up, load shapes, on-site generation, and load flexibility, none of which nominal capacity captures. Supply chain bottlenecks and permitting and siting delays could limit the modeled generation and transmission additions. The 2030 ranges are wide because they depend on project-execution assumptions. The results are only roughly consistent with LBNL's projections through 2028, which use different methods.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "EPRI projects data centers to consume 9% to 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, up from 4% to 5% today." (PDF page number not visible via web fetch; section heading: Not reported)

citation: Siddik, M. A. B., Shehabi, A., & Marston, L. (2021). The environmental footprint of data centers in the United States. Environmental Research Letters, 16(6), 064017.
region: National US (contiguous US; 2,110 8-digit HUC subbasins; electricity attributed at power control area level)
research_question: What are the spatially detailed operational water, water-scarcity, and carbon footprints of US data centers?
methodology: Bottom-up model of operational footprints for reference year 2018 (§2, p. 3). Data center locations come from Ganeshalingam et al. and commercial compilations; power plant generation and water use from EIA; emissions from EPA eGRID; water utilities from EPA SDWIS/FRS; electricity transfers from FERC Form 714 and EIA-861. Assumes direct cooling water of 1.8 m3/MWh, a cycle of concentration of 5, and annual resolution (§2.2-2.3, pp. 4-5). Facility count: Not reported.
key_findings: Total operational water footprint of 5.13 x 10^8 m3: 1.30 x 10^8 m3 direct, 3.83 x 10^8 m3 indirect from electricity generation, and 4.50 x 10^5 m3 from water and wastewater utilities (§3.1, p. 6). National average water intensity of 7.1 m3/MWh, ranging from 1.8 to 105.9 (p. 6). Water scarcity footprint of 1.29 x 10^9 m3 US-eq (p. 6). Carbon footprint of 3.15 x 10^7 t CO2-eq, nearly 0.5% of US GHG emissions (§3.3, p. 7). Data centers used 1.8% of US electricity. About one-fifth of direct water comes from moderately to highly stressed watersheds, and nearly half of servers are powered at least partly by plants in water-stressed regions (Abstract).
stated_limitations: Information on data center location and size varies by facility type and owner (§2.1, p. 3). The exact electricity each power plant supplies cannot be determined, and results are sensitive to the method used to attribute plants to consumers (§2.2, p. 4). Hydropower water assumptions are a key source of uncertainty (p. 4). The analysis runs at annual resolution only (p. 4). All data centers are assumed to use potable water (§2.3, p. 5). The national average hides large spatial variation (§3.1, p. 6). The reference year is 2018, before the growth of AI servers.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "Approximately 0.5% of total US greenhouse gas emissions are attributed to data centers." (Abstract, p. 1)

citation: Mytton, D. (2021). Data centre water consumption. npj Clean Water, 4, 11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41545-021-00101-w
research_question: How much water do data centres consume directly and indirectly, how is that consumption measured, and how good is the available data for assessing water efficiency?
methodology: Peer-reviewed narrative review (an expanded version of an earlier blog post) drawing on company disclosures, industry reports, and secondary sources. Sample size: Not reported. Time horizon: Not reported.
key_findings: US data centre water consumption is 1.7 billion litres/day, compared with total US consumption of 1,218 billion litres/day. The body text gives the underlying figure as 626 billion litres attributable to US data centres in 2014 (cited to the 2016 LBNL report), introduced under the framing that data centres consume water both indirectly through electricity generation and directly through cooling. The cited 2016 LBNL estimate includes both on-site and electricity-generation water. In some cases 57% of the water is sourced from potable supplies. Fewer than one-third of data centre operators measure water consumption. Electricity generation is the largest contributor to a data centre's water footprint. The paper proposes WUEsource, which adds water used in electricity generation to on-site WUE (L/kWh).
stated_limitations: Industry transparency is poor. Companies do not attribute their water consumption to data centres. Breakdowns by water source are missing. Unlike energy, water has no reporting requirements. Standard WUE leaves out indirect water from electricity generation. The paper's US figure rests on 2014 data from the 2016 LBNL report, not on 2021 measurements.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "Although in the USA, data centre water consumption (1.7 billion litres/day) is small compared to total water consumption (1218 billion litres/day)" (Abstract; PDF page number not visible via web fetch)

citation: Li, P., Yang, J., Islam, M. A., & Ren, S. (2023; rev. v5 2025). Making AI Less "Thirsty": Uncovering and Addressing the Secret Water Footprint of AI Models. arXiv:2304.03271 (UC Riverside). Published as Li, P., Yang, J., Islam, M. A., & Ren, S. (2025). Making AI Less 'Thirsty'. Communications of the ACM, 68(7), 54-61. https://doi.org/10.1145/3724499. Extracted from the arXiv version; the published version could not be retrieved.
region: Global, with US state-level case studies (US average, Arizona, Washington) and Ireland
research_question: How large is the on-site (scope-1) and off-site (scope-2) water footprint of AI model training and inference, and how does it vary across locations and times?
methodology: Operational water footprint = AI energy x (on-site WUE + PUE x off-site EWIF), summed over time slots. On-site PUE and WUE by location come from Microsoft disclosures. EWIF values come from WRI guidance (Reig et al., 2020). Other inputs are Google, Meta, and Equinix sustainability reports and US EIA data. Case study: GPT-3 training and inference, plus a global AI water projection for 2027 and a US on-site projection for 2028. Embodied (scope-3) water is excluded. Sample size: Not reported.
key_findings: GPT-3 training: about 5.4 million L total, including about 700,000 L of scope-1 on-site evaporation in Microsoft US data centers. GPT-3 inference: one 500 mL bottle per roughly 10-50 medium-length responses, with a US average of about 16.9 mL per request. US averages: on-site WUE 0.550 L/kWh, off-site EWIF 3.142 L/kWh, PUE 1.170. Global AI water projection for 2027: 4.2-6.6 billion m3 withdrawn and 0.38-0.60 billion m3 consumed. US data center on-site consumption in 2028: about 150-280 billion L, double to quadruple the 2023 level. One company's self-owned data centers withdrew 29 billion L and consumed more than 23 billion L in 2023, nearly 80% of it potable.
stated_limitations: Embodied water is excluded because no public scope-3 water data exists. The GPT-3 training location is not public. The inference estimate probably counts only GPU energy during token generation, so actual water use could be several times higher. No official resource-consumption data was available. The 2027 projections carry substantial uncertainty.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "For example, training the GPT-3 language model in Microsoft's state-of-the-art U.S. data centers can directly evaporate 700,000 liters of clean freshwater" (Abstract; PDF page number not visible via web fetch)

citation: Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (2024). Data Centers in Virginia (Report No. 598). Commonwealth of Virginia.
research_question: What are the economic, fiscal, energy, environmental, and water impacts of Virginia's data center industry, and does the state's sales and use tax exemption pay off?
methodology: More than 250 interviews with more than 150 stakeholders. Weldon Cooper Center produced the economic impact analysis and an independent energy demand forecast. E3 modeled future generation, transmission, emissions, and utility costs. The exemption was evaluated with FY23 tax-savings data. Energy horizon runs to 2040.
key_findings: The industry contributes 74,000 jobs, $5.5 billion in labor income, and $9.1 billion in GDP annually (p. i). Data centers and tenants reported saving $928.6 million in FY23 sales taxes through the exemption (p. 20), which about 90% of the industry uses (p. viii). The exemption returns 48 cents in revenue per $1 spent (Table 2-2, p. 23). Data center revenue ranged from less than 1% to 31% of total local revenue in five mature-market localities (p. ii). Unconstrained demand would double within 10 years (p. ii). Meeting half of it would require one 1,500 MW gas plant every two years for 15 years (p. iv). Typical Dominion residential generation and transmission costs could rise $14-$37 per month by 2040 (p. v). Diesel backup generators account for less than 4% of Northern Virginia NOx emissions (p. vi). Water use is currently sustainable but growing (p. vii). The industry used an estimated 2.1 billion gallons of water in 2023, just over a third of it reclaimed rather than new withdrawals, and less than 0.5% of total state withdrawals (p. 62). One building used 243 million gallons (10% of the industry total), and 11 buildings each used more than 50 million gallons (p. 62). At the six utilities reviewed, industry use was 0.2% to 21% of water use, excluding reclaimed water (p. 63).
stated_limitations: The energy model does not explicitly include the social cost of carbon (p. 29). The economic model omits externalities such as health and environmental costs from carbon emissions (p. 14). Average economic impacts likely underestimate more recent years because the industry is growing (p. 15). Water figures come from data shared by local utilities, at annual, monthly, or daily resolution depending on the utility (p. 102).
limitation_tags: Gross vs. Net Fiscal & Ratepayer Accounting
verbatim_quote_with_page: "contribute 74,000 jobs, $5.5 billion in labor income, and $9.1 billion in GDP" (p. i)

citation: Tarczynska, K. (2025). Cloudy Data, Costly Deals: How Poorly States Disclose Data Center Subsidies. Good Jobs First Policy Study.
region: 50 States (at least 36 with data center-specific subsidies)
research_question: Do states publicly disclose which companies receive data center subsidies, and what costs and job and investment details come with those disclosures?
methodology: Disclosure audit of state data center subsidy programs using state transparency portals and reports, the Good Jobs First Subsidy Tracker, Nevada's legislative abatement report, Policy Matters Ohio, earlier Good Jobs First studies, and news coverage. No formal methodology is stated. Time horizon: Not reported.
key_findings: At least 36 states have data center-specific subsidies. 11 disclose recipients, 24 do not, and Kansas was too new to assess (pp. 2, 5-6). 5 states disclose subsidy amounts, 4 disclose promised jobs, and none reports both promised and actual jobs (pp. 2, 9). 6 states disclose capital investment (p. 10). Texas spent about $1 billion in FY2025 and Virginia abated nearly $1 billion in state and local sales and use tax (p. 2). Illinois forwent $370 million in 2024, and ten states each lose more than $100 million per year (p. 4). Virginia loses about 52 cents per dollar of exemption; Washington and Georgia lose roughly 60-70 cents (pp. 3, 5). Cost per job: Illinois averages $1.4 million; Nevada's Switch deal $2.1 million (2016); Ohio $1.4 million for Google and $1 million for Meta (pp. 13-14). Nine states include property tax exemptions (p. 4).
stated_limitations: Disclosure is too poor for meaningful analysis or cross-state comparison (p. 13). Some disclosed data is outdated, such as Ohio's Amazon figures (p. 8). Nevada's outcome data lags approvals by years (p. 11). Jobs are not broken down by type, wage, or hiring location (pp. 9-10). Cost-per-job figures exist for only a few cases (p. 13). The Georgia figure appears without a unit, likely a typo (p. 6).
limitation_tags: Gross vs. Net Fiscal & Ratepayer Accounting
verbatim_quote_with_page: "At least 36 states have economic development subsidies specifically crafted for data center projects," (p. 2)

citation: Regional Economic Models, Inc. / U.S. Chamber of Commerce [Dubay, C.] (2026). The Economic and Community Impacts of Data Centers. Regional Economic Models, Inc.
region: 50 States, plus four representative counties for tax analysis (incl. Franklin County, OH and Dallas County, TX)
research_question: What economic, employment, and tax revenue impacts does one new 50 MW data center generate in its host state and county?
methodology: REMI PI+ model (input-output, CGE, econometric, and economic geography methods). 50 state scenarios, each modeling one hypothetical 50 MW facility. Two-year construction phase and 20-year operating period. Assumes $1.69 billion in construction spending, 50 on-site workers per year plus utility staffing, and $1 billion in equipment replacement every five years. County tax revenue is estimated by applying tax rates to REMI outputs.
key_findings: Average annual host-state impacts, construction phase: 5,220 jobs, $680 million state GDP, $400 million personal income. Operational phase: 740 jobs, $175 million GDP, $125 million personal income. Nationwide during construction: about 10,600 jobs and $1.6 billion GDP per year. Five-year gross county tax revenue ranges from about $96 million (Franklin County, OH) to $174 million (Dallas County, TX). Employment figures are economy-wide, not on-site. Explicit multipliers: Not reported (none appear on either the REMI study page or the U.S. Chamber of Commerce report page).
stated_limitations: Results are statewide, economy-wide estimates, not facility-specific forecasts. Tax figures are approximate gross revenue, not net fiscal benefits. Actual collections depend on local tax rules, depreciation, exemptions, and negotiated abatements. Electricity demand, water, land use, traffic, and noise costs are mentioned but not quantified. Authorship is inconsistent across sources: the REMI page lists the U.S. Department of Commerce, the study text credits Curtis Dubay of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, and the Chamber's own page (dated October 15, 2026) names no individual author.
limitation_tags: Gross vs. Net Fiscal & Ratepayer Accounting
verbatim_quote_with_page: "These figures are approximate gross revenue estimates, rather than net fiscal benefits." (Section: Data Center Tax Revenue and Fiscal Impacts; no PDF page numbers on the REMI web page)

citation: Martin, E., & Peskoe, A. (2025). Extracting Profits from the Public: How Utility Ratepayers Are Paying for Big Tech's Power. Harvard Law School, Environmental and Energy Law Program, Electricity Law Initiative.
region: United States (state public utility commission and federal proceedings; examples from the PJM region, including Virginia and Maryland)
research_question: How are utilities shifting the costs of data centers' electricity use onto other ratepayers through special contracts, tariffs, transmission cost allocation, and co-location arrangements?
methodology: Legal and regulatory analysis based on a review of nearly 50 regulatory proceedings about data centers' rates (p. 2), including 40 state PUC proceedings about special contracts with data centers (p. 11), plus PJM transmission cost allocation and FERC co-location proceedings (pp. 15, 20-21). No original quantitative model.
key_findings: Regulators frequently approve data center special contracts in short and conclusory orders, with few or no other parties participating and with confidential treatment of the contracts (p. 11). In December 2023 PJM approved $5 billion of transmission projects driven in part by data center load growth; about half of the cost was assigned to Virginia utilities and about 10% to Maryland utilities (p. 15). Maryland's three investor-owned utilities assign an average of 66% of transmission costs to residential ratepayers, and the larger Virginia investor-owned utility puts more than half in residential rates (p. 15). Exelon estimated that a single proposed nuclear co-location arrangement would shift $58 million to $140 million of transmission and distribution charges to other ratepayers; generators dispute the estimate (p. 20). Litigation showed Duke Energy planned to shift the cost of a $325 million special-contract discount to its other ratepayers (p. 13; the contract was not identified as a data center contract). Total quantified ratepayer cost shift: Not reported.
stated_limitations: The authors state that verifying utility claims that data center costs are isolated from other ratepayers is all but impossible, because cost attribution is imprecise and contracts are often confidential (pp. 1-2). They acknowledge that a data center under a special contract could, in theory, be overpaying (p. 13). Utilities often decline to disclose facility-specific load forecasts as proprietary (p. 5). The co-location cost-shift figure is Exelon's estimate and is disputed by generators (p. 20). Written as legal and policy analysis with recommendations, not as a neutral audit.
limitation_tags: Gross vs. Net Fiscal & Ratepayer Accounting
verbatim_quote_with_page: "Hiding subsidies for trillion-dollar companies in power prices increases utility profits by raising costs for American consumers." (p. 1)

citation: Monitoring Analytics, LLC (Independent Market Monitor for PJM) (2026). 2026 Quarterly State of the Market Report for PJM: January through September. Section 1: Introduction.
research_question: How competitive and reliable were PJM's wholesale power markets in the first nine months of 2026, and what has including forecast data center load in the capacity market cost customers?
methodology: Independent Market Monitor review of PJM energy and capacity market results for January through September 2026, compared with the same period of 2025 (pp. 1-3). Data center cost impacts draw on the Monitor's analyses of the 2025/2026 through 2028/2029 Base Residual Auctions (p. 51). Only Section 1 (Introduction) was retrieved and reviewed.
key_findings: The results of the 2025/2026, 2026/2027, 2027/2028, and 2028/2029 capacity markets were not competitive, primarily because forecast data center demand was included (p. 1). Including data center load in the capacity market auctions has resulted in an irreversible total increase in capacity costs of $29.4 billion for all customers (pp. 1, 51). The total cost of wholesale power rose 40.9%, from $79.19 to $111.61 per MWh, between the first nine months of 2025 and of 2026; $9.95 per MWh (9.8%) of the 2026 cost is attributed to including data center load in the capacity market (p. 3). The 2029/2030 auction is expected to add another $5 billion to $10 billion of data center related costs (p. 1). PJM's capacity shortfall grew from 208.7 MW in the 2026/2027 auction to 6,516.6 MW in 2027/2028 and 6,831.3 MW in 2028/2029 (p. 1).
stated_limitations: The Monitor describes data center load forecasts as largely based on unsubstantiated forecasts, and notes the 2029/2030 auction will use a 2026 load forecast that includes data centers already canceled or unlikely to reach projected demand (pp. 1-2). The $29.4 billion figure comes from the Monitor's auction analyses rather than observed customer bills. Only Section 1 of the report was retrieved. Facility-level data center load: Not reported.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "the inclusion of data center load in the capacity market auctions has resulted in an irreversible total increase in capacity costs of $29.4 billion" (p. 51)

citation: Justice, J. S., & Shepherd, T. L. (2025). Tax Incentive Evaluation: Georgia Data Center Sales & Use Tax Exemption. University of Georgia, Carl Vinson Institute of Government, for the Georgia Department of Audits and Accounts (DOAA summary revised January 2026).
region: Georgia (statewide; local property tax sample from four metro Atlanta projects)
research_question: What revenue does Georgia forgo through its data center sales and use tax exemption, and what economic impact and return on investment does the exemption produce?
methodology: Statutory tax incentive evaluation under SB 366 (p. 2). Georgia Department of Revenue data on 34 data centers using or applying for the exemption, plus a nationwide Aterio database of active, under-construction, and announced data centers (pp. 2-3). An econometric 'but for' model attributes 30% of data center activity to the exemption (p. 3). IMPLAN 2023 input-output modeling of construction and operations, 2018-2030, with some years estimated rather than reported (pp. 3-5). Local property tax analysis combines four metro Atlanta projects (nine buildings, $6.5 billion investment) into one representative complex (p. 46).
key_findings: Forgone state tax revenue was $474.2 million in 2025, projected to reach $866.7 million in 2030 (Table A, p. 5). After the 30% 'but for' adjustment, added state tax collections in 2025 were $34.6 million from construction and equipment and $6.9 million from operations, for a net fiscal impact of -$432.6 million (Table A, p. 5; Table A reports -$432,641,337, and the components rounded to one decimal sum to -$432.7 million). Net fiscal impact ranges from -$17.0 million in 2018 to -$780.2 million in 2030 (p. 4). The projected overall 2018-2030 return on investment is 186.3%, or about $2.86 of value-added impact per $1 of forgone revenue, versus $1.32 under an alternate-use scenario (p. 7). A representative metro Atlanta complex valued at $2.28 billion would owe $33.6 million a year in local property tax; the average abatement was 17.3%, leaving $27.8 million collected (pp. 46-47). Additional data centers could raise statewide electricity demand by 49% between 2025 and 2030 (p. 45).
stated_limitations: The 30% 'but for' attribution differs substantially from the 2022 predecessor study, which assumed 90% of data center activity was due to the exemption; the 2022 study lacked Department of Revenue data and relied on external sources (pp. 2-3, 6). Some years use Institute estimates instead of reported data because of unfiled and amended annual reports (pp. 3-4). Projections assume current construction trends continue, and changes in AI investment could produce substantially different results (p. 7). Complete and verified statewide data center electricity use is not yet publicly available (p. 9), and the electricity projections cannot address local or seasonal supply imbalances (p. 44). Local abatement data covers four metro Atlanta projects, and available data cannot show how effective abatements were in attracting them (pp. 46, 48). Grid and water strain are described as intangible effects and are not quantified (p. 9). Water volumes: Not reported.
limitation_tags: Gross vs. Net Fiscal & Ratepayer Accounting
verbatim_quote_with_page: "The net fiscal impact of Georgia’s High-Tech Data Center Equipment Exemption ranges from -$17.0 million in 2018 to -$780.2 million in 2030." (p. 4)

citation: COMPASS Research Consortium, Bureau of Economic Geology, University of Texas at Austin (2026). Water Use Requirements for Data Centers in Texas: A White Paper on the Evolving Demands of Water Use in Data Center Infrastructure in Texas. Originally published December 2025; last updated August 2026.
research_question: How much direct and indirect water could Texas data centers use from 2025 to 2040, and how does that compare with statewide water demand?
methodology: Screening-level, scenario-based engineering assessment (p. 24). An assumed 8 GW of capacity for 2025 and capacity scenarios of 40-70 GW for 2030 and 60-110 GW for 2040; three facility-performance cases varying utilization, PUE, and WUE; and three representative ERCOT grid-mix scenarios for indirect water (pp. 25-26). Shares are compared against the 2022 Texas Water Development Board State Water Plan (p. 24). Uses publicly available assumptions rather than operator data (p. 24).
key_findings: Average total (direct plus indirect) water use of 33 billion gallons in 2025 (0.6% of statewide demand), 225 billion gallons in 2030 (3.7%), and 348 billion gallons in 2040 (5.8%); direct water alone is 13 billion gallons (0.2%), 90 billion gallons (1.5%), and 139 billion gallons (2.3%) (Table 7, pp. 24-25). Under ERCOT's adjusted 2030 capacity estimate of 22 GW, total water use is about 91 billion gallons (1.5%); under the 78 GW transmission-provider estimate it is about 319 billion gallons (5.3%) (p. 25). The 2025 total is described as consistent in magnitude with an independent assessment of 25 billion gallons, or 0.4% (p. 4). Indirect water use often takes the major share of the total (p. 26).
stated_limitations: Estimates are indicative rather than predictive (p. 25). Assumed data center capacity is the single largest source of uncertainty; for 2030, transmission providers reported 78 GW of prospective large-load capacity while ERCOT's adjusted estimate is 22 GW (p. 26). Facility-level, operator-reported water-use data were not available (p. 24). Indirect water may already be counted in the State Water Plan's steam-electric category, so totals should not be added to statewide demand (p. 26). 2025 shares are expressed against the Plan's 2020 estimate because the Plan has no 2025 column (p. 24).
verbatim_quote_with_page: "average total water use increases from 33 billion gallons per year in 2025 (0.6% of statewide demand) to 225 billion gallons in 2030 (3.7%)" (p. 25)

citation: Cook, M. (2026). Thirsty Data and the Lone Star State: The Impact of Data Center Growth on Texas' Water Supply. Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) White Paper.
research_question: How much water do Texas data centers consume directly and through electricity generation today, and how could that change by 2030 under different power-supply choices?
methodology: Top-down estimate. Existing capacity of about 9,567 MW across 464 Texas facilities from Baxtel (p. 7). Direct water at LBNL's 2023 rate of 95 gal/MWh; indirect water from 2023 Texas power plant withdrawal and consumption data reported to the EIA on forms 923 and 860 (p. 10). 2030 projections use ERCOT's adjusted (22,175 MW) and transmission-provider (77,965 MW) data center forecasts, LBNL's 2028 rate of 119-127 gal/MWh, and four power-supply scenarios (pp. 11-12). Shares are compared with the 2022 State Water Plan (p. 10).
key_findings: Existing Texas data centers consume an estimated 25 billion gallons (77 thousand acre-feet) of water in 2025, or 0.4% of total water use, combining on-site cooling and power-plant consumption (pp. 4, 6). Direct cooling is about 8 billion gallons (0.1%) and power-plant consumption about 17 billion gallons (0.3%), while the grid power supplying the data centers withdraws about 1,067 billion gallons a year (p. 10). By 2030, demand could reach 29-161 billion gallons, 0.5-2.7% of total annual water use (pp. 4, 6). Power supply choice changes the result: new grid power cuts water use 54% and onsite natural gas combined-cycle power 30% compared with current grid power (p. 13). Texas' State Water Plan does not include projected demand growth for data centers (p. 4).
stated_limitations: Transparency issues have made data center water use difficult to determine (p. 6), and data center water and energy information is significantly limited (p. 5). Estimates apply LBNL national water rates to capacity figures rather than facility data (pp. 10-11). Carbon capture is not included (p. 11). The report states the 2030 range three ways: 29-161 billion gallons (98-494 kAF) on p. 4, 29-161 billion gallons (88-494 kAF) on p. 6, and 23-161 billion gallons (71-494 kAF), or 0.4-2.7%, on p. 12.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "In this paper, we estimate that Texas data centers in 2025 will consume a total of 25 billion gallons (Bgal) of water" (p. 6)

citation: Ceres (2026). Water Behind the Watts: The Hidden Risk of Powering Data Centers. Ceres, August 2026.
region: Seven states: Virginia, Texas, California, Illinois, Georgia, Ohio, and Arizona (about 50% of US data centers)
research_question: How much freshwater is withdrawn to generate the electricity that powers data centers in seven major states, and how exposed are those power plants to water stress and drought?
methodology: Power plant analysis of 2024 EIA forms 860 and 923. Of 3,907 plants with active 2024 generation, 1,434 water-using plants were analyzed; 194 reported water data to EIA and 1,240 were estimated with WRI technology-specific withdrawal factors (pp. 6, 18). Water is attributed to data centers using EPRI's 2024 state-level estimates of data centers' electricity share (pp. 6, 18). Water stress from WRI Aqueduct 4.0 and drought from the 2024 U.S. Drought Monitor (p. 18). Measures withdrawals, not consumption, and counts hydropower as a withdrawal (pp. 2, 6, 18).
key_findings: Powering data centers in the seven states used an estimated 3.4 trillion gallons of water withdrawals in 2024, ranging from 25 billion gallons in Ohio to 1.4 trillion gallons in California (p. 7). 78% of the electricity in the states analyzed came from power plants that use water to operate, and Ohio, Georgia, and Virginia each generated over 90% of their electricity from water-intensive thermal plants (p. 3). 66% of water-using power plants were exposed to medium-high to extremely high water stress (p. 3). On-site data center water and water consumption: Not reported (the analysis covers withdrawals for purchased electricity only).
stated_limitations: Findings are directional estimates, not precise measurements (p. 18). Water data is self-reported to EIA and not independently verified, and plants without reported data use WRI national-average factors (pp. 18-19). Embedded water is estimated from state-level generation rather than balancing-authority dispatch and is attributed where electricity is generated, so exporting states may be overstated and importing states such as Virginia and California understated (p. 19). Behind-the-meter generation, water sources, and seasonal variation are outside scope (p. 6). The key findings page gives drought exposure both as 46% of water-using plants and as 44% of electricity generated using water (p. 3). Published by an investor-advocacy nonprofit.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "Powering data centers used an estimated 3.4 trillion gallons of water withdrawals in 2024, applying EPRI state estimates." (p. 7)

citation: Watten, A., Bistline, J., & Blanford, G. (2026). Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill? Causal Evidence from the United States. EPRI white paper, arXiv:2606.19777v1 (summarized in an EPRI ESCA brief, June 2026).
region: United States (state-level panel; 366 large investor-owned utilities for the cost analysis)
research_question: Did data center growth raise or lower average retail electricity prices in the United States from 2015 to 2024?
methodology: Instrumental-variables (two-stage least squares) regression of state residential revenue on data center capacity additions, conditional on residential sales, 2015-2024 (pp. 9, 13-14). The instrument is the length of the 1947 Interstate Highway Plan in each state, conditional on GDP and population (p. 3). Retail revenue and sales from EIA Form 861 bundled providers (93% of residential sales); data center capacity additions from S&P Global; utility cost data from FERC Form 1 for 366 investor-owned utilities (69% of retail sales) (pp. 7-8). Data center power use is not observed and is assumed at 50% of capacity (p. 13).
key_findings: A doubling of data center capacity caused residential retail prices to fall by 3.5% for a fixed level of residential demand, with an Anderson-Rubin interval of -12.1% to -1.4% (p. 21); equivalently, about 0.4% lower prices per 10% more capacity (p. 3). From 2019 to 2024 the average residential customer lived in a state where data center capacity grew 160%, which caused rates to fall by 6% (p. 3). Restricting the sample to 2019-2024 halves the estimated effect, and first-difference estimates are precisely zero (p. 21). Effects on commercial and industrial prices are substantially smaller than for residential prices (p. 22). Transmission, distribution, and generation costs show economies of scale (p. 1). Wholesale prices and capacity-market costs: Not reported.
stated_limitations: The authors caution that future supply constraints could reverse the effect (p. 1), grouping caveats into supply constraints, durability of demand growth, and fuel costs (p. 22). Data center power use is not observed (p. 13). The instrument is weak in the neighboring-state spillover specification (first-stage F of 0.6) (pp. 21-22). Data end in 2024. The EPRI brief rounds the 3.5% estimate to roughly 4%.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "a doubling of data center capacity causes residential retail prices to fall by 3.5% for a fixed level of residential demand" (p. 21)

citation: Kay, O., Reaser, R., & Taylor, R. (2026). Processing Power: The Effect of Data Centers on Wholesale Electricity Markets. Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Working Paper 2606, March 2026, revised October 2026. https://doi.org/10.24149/wp2606r1 (an earlier draft, dated April 28, 2026, circulated as an NBER conference paper).
region: Continental United States (23 regional markets based on eGRID subregions)
research_question: How has data center load growth affected wholesale electricity prices, generator payments, and carbon emissions in the United States, how could it affect them through 2028, and when can load growth lower retail rates?
methodology: Hourly, unit-level dispatch model in which 23 U.S. regional markets trade over capacity-constrained interfaces (Abstract), covering 2021-2025 and a 2026-2028 forecast (p. 37). Supply comes from EPA CEMS combustion units over 25 MW, not nuclear or renewable generators (p. 10). Because utilization is not observed, outcomes are compared with no-data-center counterfactuals under several utilization scenarios (pp. 2, 15); new capacity is scaled to 40% of announced capacity in the mid-range and low scenarios (p. 17). A fixed-cost-spreading framework derives when load growth can lower retail rates (pp. 51-56).
key_findings: Data centers raised wholesale prices by 6.9% nationally by 2025 and by 15.0% in northern Virginia; under the preferred scenario the national effect reaches 12.3% by 2028 (Abstract). ERCOT has a smaller price effect despite the second-highest data center capacity (p. 28). Data centers increased total payments to generators by $96.5 billion over 2021-2025 (p. 34); in restructured markets, wholesale consumers paid generators $62.6 billion more from 2021 to 2025 in the mid-peak scenario (p. 35). Over 2021-2028, payments rise by about $186.7 billion, of which $94.5 billion (about 50%) are inframarginal rents (p. 3), and production costs rise by $87.9 billion (p. 35). By the end of 2025, data centers generated 8.9 to 28.1 million additional tons of CO2 per month (p. 36; short tons per Figure 8), or $24 billion to $75 billion in damages a year at a $224 social cost of carbon (pp. 36-37). Accounting for spillovers, many regions have offset ratios above one, meaning load growth cannot lower retail rates there even without added system costs (p. 56).
stated_limitations: Actual utilization factors are unknown (p. 15). Power plant entry and exit are treated as exogenous (p. 42); against an endogenous-supply case, the main result overstates price effects by at most 2.44 percentage points (p. 43). Only grid emissions are counted; behind-the-meter and backup generation are excluded (p. 37). The retail analysis assumes no added fixed costs and likely understates retail price effects (p. 51). CEMS excludes nuclear and renewable generators (p. 10). Working paper, not peer-reviewed; the revised figures differ from the April 2026 NBER draft.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "Data centers raised wholesale prices by 6.9 percent nationally by 2025 and by 15.0 percent in northern Virginia" (Abstract)

citation: Han, Y., Wu, Z., Li, P., Wierman, A., & Ren, S. (2024; rev. v4 2026). Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers. arXiv:2412.06288v4 (v1 December 2024; v4 June 8, 2026).
region: Contiguous United States (county level; backup-generator analysis for Virginia)
research_question: What criteria air pollutant emissions and public health costs do U.S. data centers cause, and how could computing be managed to reduce them?
methodology: Emissions for 2023 and 2028 are entered into EPA's COBRA Desktop v5.1 screening model to estimate county-level health outcomes and costs, in 2023 dollars at a 2% discount rate (pp. 3-4). Scope-1 backup-generator emissions come from Virginia permits, with a reference case at 10% of permitted levels and Virginia's rate applied to other states (pp. 4-5). Scope-2 power-plant emissions are attributed by grid region using EPRI's 2023 state distribution of data center electricity scaled to LBNL national totals (p. 5). 2028 uses LBNL's low- and high-growth scenarios (p. 7).
key_findings: In 2023, U.S. data centers caused an estimated $6.67 billion ($5.03-$8.32 billion) in public health costs and 433 deaths, 1.31% of U.S. fuel-combustion health costs; power-plant (scope-2) costs of $6.16 billion dominate backup-generator (scope-1) costs of $0.51 billion (Table 1, p. 7). Costs reach $11.7 billion and $20.9 billion in 2028 under low and high growth, increases of 75% and 213% against a 17% rise for fuel combustion overall (p. 8). The high-growth 2028 case includes about 600,000 asthma symptom cases and 1,300 premature deaths (p. 8). The highest county-level per-household health cost is about seven times the national average and about 200 times the lowest (pp. 2, 6). Virginia backup generators could cause $220-300 million a year in health costs in the reference case (p. 5).
stated_limitations: COBRA is a screening model and cannot replace more sophisticated air quality models (p. 3). Baseline emissions come from EPA projections, and regulatory changes since then may introduce substantial uncertainty (p. 5). Scope-1 results assume emissions at 10% of permitted levels and apply Virginia's rate to other states (pp. 4-5). Results are county-level only (p. 7). Preprint, not peer-reviewed; extracted from v4.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "Our findings suggest that the total annual public health burden of U.S. data centers could exceed $20 billion in 2028 under the high-growth scenario." (p. 11)

citation: James, K., Perveen, S., & Jacobson, B. (2025). Drained by Data: The Cumulative Impact of Data Centers on Regional Water Stress. Ceres, September 2025 (research and analysis by Bluerisk). Companion to ceres_2026.
region: Phoenix, Arizona region (Arizona Public Service and Salt River Project service areas and nearby water basins)
research_question: How much direct and indirect water do current and planned data centers in the Phoenix region use, and how much could they raise regional water stress?
methodology: Inventory of 124 current and planned Phoenix-area data centers from Data Center Map, company websites, utility websites, and company disclosures, characterized by size, IT capacity, cooling technology, PUE, and WUE, with missing values imputed from facility size, cooling type, and industry averages (pp. 7, 15). Water use equals IT capacity times load factor times on-site WUE, plus electricity-related water from 2023 EIA forms 860 and 923 power mix and withdrawal intensities for APS and SRP (p. 15). Load factors from the 2024 US Data Center Energy Usage Report (p. 15). Water stress from WRI Aqueduct 4.0 baseline data, holding other sectors' demand and supply constant (pp. 15-16).
key_findings: Annual water use associated with data center electricity is expected to rise 400%, from an estimated 2.9 billion gallons to over 14.5 billion gallons, if planned data centers come online over the next six years (pp. 3, 7). Direct cooling water is estimated at 385 million gallons a year, rising 870% to more than 3.7 billion gallons (pp. 3, 8). Annual water stress could rise 17% in the Hassayampa basin (22% in August), 2% in the Centennial Wash basin (9% in December and January), and up to 32% in the Chaco basin, which is not currently classed as water-stressed (pp. 8-9). Phoenix-area IT capacity is projected to grow 324%, from 1,193 MW to 5,057 MW (p. 7).
stated_limitations: Holding other sectors' demand and water supply constant means the stress increases are likely underestimated (p. 16). Missing PUE and WUE values are imputed (pp. 7, 15). The 2023 power mix and withdrawal intensities are held unchanged for the future (p. 15). Electricity-related water excludes water used to extract, process, and transport coal and gas (p. 7). The executive summary gives water stress increases of up to 17% (p. 3), while p. 8 gives up to 32% for the Chaco basin. Electricity-related water is described as withdrawals (p. 7) and as consumption (p. 15). Pages 6-16 have no text layer and were read from rendered page images. Published by an investor-advocacy nonprofit.
verbatim_quote_with_page: "annual water use associated with data center electricity consumption is expected to increase by 400%, from an estimated 2.9 billion gallons" (p. 3)
